topic: How do large language models resolve parametric vs. contextual knowledge conflicts in RAG when retrieved information contradicts pre-trained weights, and how effective are decoding-time interventions?
hypothesis: Large language models tend to favor pre-trained parametric knowledge over contradictory retrieved context unless specific decoding-time interventions are applied to adjust attention weights or probability distributions, and the effectiveness of such interventions varies significantly depending on model scale and prompt structure.
competing_hypotheses: Models prioritize retrieved contextual knowledge over parametric memory by default when retrieval scores exceed a certain confidence threshold without requiring decoding-time interventions.
Decoding-time interventions provide negligible improvement in conflict resolution compared to instruction tuning and model alignment techniques.
Conflict resolution behavior is entirely unpredictable and driven by superficial token overlap rather than semantic alignment between parametric weights and retrieved context.
falsification_criteria: Empirical evaluations demonstrating that baseline unprompted models reliably follow contradictory context across diverse scales without degradation.
Studies showing that decoding-time interventions introduce catastrophic degradation on standard benchmarks without improving factual conflict resolution.
Evidence that models universally ignore parametric weights when any external context is supplied.
evaluation_criteria: Conflict resolution rate: the percentage of generations where the model successfully adopts the correct contradictory retrieved context over pre-trained parametric memory.
Faithfulness metric: the degree to which generated outputs reflect the retrieved evidence rather than internal hallucinations or priors.
Downstream performance degradation: the drop in general benchmark accuracy when decoding-time interventions are applied to resolve knowledge conflicts.

evidence_sufficiency.medium: Useful empirical evidence exists from preprints or technical reports, but coverage or baseline comparisons are limited.
evidence_sufficiency.high: Multiple strong independent peer-reviewed sources agree on the underlying mechanism and report consistent quantitative improvements across standard benchmarks.
evidence_sufficiency.low: Evidence is sparse, indirect, or restricted to narrow toy models without rigorous evaluation.
evidence_sufficiency.conflicting: Comparable empirical studies support materially different conclusions regarding the efficacy of decoding-time interventions.
evidence_sufficiency.insufficient: Available evidence cannot justify any conclusion regarding how models resolve parametric versus contextual conflicts.
